quote: Man muss dann weiter fragen welche Functionen von den Lösungen der linearen Differentialgleichungen wiederum denselben genügen.
english: One must then further ask which functions of the solutions of the linear differential equations again satisfy the same equations.
topic: The page ends a note on functions of solutions of linear differential equations, proposing the case n=3 and physics equations as leads, then gives an analogy that ideal theory is like a fast steamer reaching a goal more quickly than a long chain of elementary procedures.

triage.modern_statement: The question is: given a linear ODE L(y)=0 of order n with a fundamental system y1,…,yn, which functions F(y1,…,yn) (most naturally polynomial or rational ones, possibly also involving derivatives) again satisfy L or another linear differential equation over the same coefficient field? Today this belongs to Picard–Vessiot (differential Galois) theory. Products of solutions satisfy symmetric powers or symmetric products of L. A rational expression in the solutions lies in the base field exactly when the differential Galois group leaves it unchanged. Polynomial relations among the solutions, and invariants or semi-invariants of the Galois group, are what decide whether such a function satisfies a lower-order equation or is rational or algebraic. Hilbert's suggested test case n=3 matches the classical work of Fuchs and Fano on third-order equations whose solutions satisfy homogeneous polynomial relations.
triage.answered_by: No single answer. The question was absorbed into the Galois theory of linear differential equations: Émile Picard proposed it in 1883, Vessiot developed it in the 1890s, and Kolchin gave it a rigorous footing with algebraic groups in 1948. For order 3, Fano's classical work (c. 1900) on solutions satisfying polynomial relations was later made precise by the Fano–Singer theorem. In computer algebra, symmetric powers and invariants of differential Galois groups (Singer, Ulmer, van Hoeij and others, 1990s onward) give algorithms for exactly this kind of question.

evidence.claim: Archibald's history of French work on this, 1880–1910, says Émile Picard first proposed a 'Galois theory' of differential equations in 1883.
Picard–Vessiot theory, beginning in 1883, is the Galois theory of the differential field extensions that come from linear differential equations.
Kolchin, in 1948, was the first to put differential Galois theory on a modern, rigorous footing.

The symmetric power or symmetric product of operators is the smallest operator whose solutions include the products y1*y2 of solutions. There are algorithms to compute invariants of the differential Galois group from such constructions.

Fano–Singer theorem: if the solutions of an order-n operator lie on a curve, then after a shift either all solutions are algebraic or L is the (n-1)th symmetric power of a second-order operator. This is the n=3 situation Hilbert points to.
Singer and Ulmer showed that Liouvillian solutions of L(y)=0 are tied to semi-invariant forms of the differential Galois group that factor into linear forms.

triage.why: Hilbert's sentence is a general programmatic question, not a sharp conjecture, and it is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The best match is the classical question of which functions of solutions satisfy linear ODEs again. Picard–Vessiot theory, the invariant theory of differential Galois groups, and symmetric powers answer that in principle. The n=3 case Hilbert mentions matches the Fuchs/Fano studies of third-order equations, which the Fano–Singer theorem later settled. The field is still active: computing Galois groups and invariants, and solving equations in terms of lower-order ones. However, I found no source that discusses Hilbert's note itself, so linking it to this theory is my own reading and the identification is uncertain.
